title: 25 Years After 9/11, Could Afghanistan Again Become A Launchpad For Global Terror?
gist: Twenty-five years after 9/11, Al-Qaeda operatives again have safe haven in Taliban-run Afghanistan, with UN reporting describing the country as the group's 'symbolic homeland' - yet no major Western attack has been plotted from there. Experts split between a 'ticking bomb' read and the view that the Taliban are self-deterred and the real Al-Qaeda threat has migrated to Africa, with US intelligence coverage too degraded to tell which is right.

themes.theme: Full circle: Al-Qaeda's return under Taliban rule

insights.claim: A December 2025 United Nations sanctions team report described Afghanistan as the 'symbolic homeland' for Al-Qaeda and documented personal relationships and intermarriages between Al-Qaeda and Taliban members.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Institutional UN documentation of group fusion is the evidentiary basis for any future re-designation or sanctions tightening on Kabul.

insights.claim: Afghanistan is already harboring terrorists with international aspirations, and the open question is only whether they act on them.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Frames the risk as intent-limited rather than capability-limited, which makes it a step-function rather than gradual threat.
insights.quote: It is already harboring terrorists who have international aspirations. The next question is going to be whether they're going to carry those out.

insights.claim: Expecting the Taliban to honor the 2020 Doha commitments is self-delusion because they are a terrorist organization, and the policy response should be weakening the government in Kabul.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: A hawkish former national security adviser arguing for active pressure signals a live constituency against any normalization or sanctions relief.
insights.quote: What we should be doing is weakening the terrorist government in Afghanistan.
insights.locator: General HR McMaster, who served as US national-security adviser

insights.claim: The 2020 agreement traded international force withdrawal for a Taliban pledge not to let Al-Qaeda or others use Afghan soil against the US and allies, including a ban on recruiting, training and fundraising.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: The text of the deal is the benchmark against which any future US enforcement action will be justified.
insights.locator: In 2020, during Donald Trump's first term

insights.claim: Al-Qaeda is not the only dangerous group operating with Taliban blessing: it has worked with Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan on cross-border attacks into Pakistan, and Islamic State militants are present and attacking in both Afghanistan and Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: The nearest-term realized risk is Pakistani, not Western, which matters for Pakistan security and sovereign risk.

insights.claim: Afghanistan today is a witch's brew of militant groups that resembles a ticking bomb.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: The maximal-threat framing from a specialist think tank is the case to watch for a shift in US policy if any attack materializes.
insights.locator: Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center

insights.claim: Twenty-five years after 9/11 and five years after the Taliban takeover, no major terrorist act in Western capitals has been plotted from Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: The absence of realized attacks is the strongest empirical argument against re-escalating US involvement in Afghanistan.
insights.locator: So far, this has not led to major terror acts

insights.claim: A major difference from the pre-9/11 period is that the Taliban themselves lived through 9/11 and its consequences, giving them reason to keep a close eye on what Al-Qaeda members in Afghanistan are doing.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Self-deterrence through learned experience is the key mechanism behind the low-threat case; it breaks if Taliban leadership fragments.
insights.quote: A major difference now relative to pre-9/11 is that the Taliban lived through the experience of 9/11 and the ramifications that that brought

insights.claim: The absence of terrorism after five years of Taliban rule indicates genuine change, and there is little evidence that Al-Qaeda is organizing, fundraising or training on Afghan territory.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to UN reporting from a former Joint Chiefs strategy adviser; the expert consensus is genuinely split, so headlines will whipsaw.
insights.quote: there is little evidence to suggest that Al-Qaeda is organizing, fundraising, or training on Afghan territory
insights.locator: Carter Malkasian, a former special assistant for strategy

insights.claim: The Taliban are actively pursuing international legitimacy, recently sending a delegation to meet the European Union in Brussels and having been recognized by Russia as Afghanistan's legitimate government, though Western outreach stays cool over women's rights and human rights abuses.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Creeping recognition is the channel through which Afghan assets, aviation and trade restrictions could eventually loosen; Russia set the precedent.
insights.locator: The group is now actively reaching out

insights.claim: The most virulent, active and violent Al-Qaeda affiliates today are in Africa - Al-Shabaab and various West African groups carrying an Al-Qaeda affiliation - not in Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Counterterrorism attention and risk premia should follow the Sahel and Horn of Africa, not Central Asia.
insights.quote: If you're trying to combat the most virulent Al-Qaeda affiliates at this point in time, those exist in Africa, whether it's Al-Shabaab or the West African various groups that carry an Al-Qaeda affiliation.
insights.locator: Schroden, who is finalizing a book

insights.claim: The latest US Counterterrorism Strategy, published in May 2026, emphasizes threats from Africa and other geographic areas rather than Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Official strategy documents drive resource allocation; expect US CT spending and partnerships to tilt toward Africa.
insights.locator: The latest US Counterterrorism Strategy, published in May

themes.theme: Intelligence blindness as the real risk

insights.claim: Washington's ability to monitor Afghanistan is far weaker than in 2020 let alone 2011, and the US may simply be unable to detect terrorist plotting and training in mountain villages or the backstreets of Kabul, Kandahar or Jalalabad.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Low observed threat may be a measurement artifact; this asymmetry means surprise risk is skewed to the downside.
insights.quote: Washington's ability to monitor Afghanistan is not what it was in 2020, let alone 2011. The United States may be unable to detect terrorist plotting and training in mountain villages or in the backstreets of Kabul, Kandahar, or Jalalabad
insights.locator: Malkasian, who was a political officer in Helmand

insights.claim: There has been no US strike in Afghanistan since Al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahri was killed in Kabul in 2022, which means either the US lacks the insight to generate targets or the high-value targets no longer exist.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: A clean binary test for the state of over-the-horizon counterterrorism; resolving it either way would move Afghan policy sharply.
insights.quote: Either the US has so little insight into what's happening there that it can't generate targets to strike, or there just aren't the types of high-value targets to strike in Afghanistan today as there once were
insights.locator: This was a point picked up by Schroden

insights.claim: Even Malkasian, who disputes the UN reporting on Al-Qaeda, acknowledges that the underlying intelligence is patchy.
insights.speaker: Ray Furlong
insights.so_what: Both sides of the debate rest on thin evidence, so confidence intervals on Afghan terror risk are wide in both directions.
insights.locator: but acknowledged that intelligence was patchy
